summary: Defines a DHCP option that carries a list of pointers to servers for The Open Group's User Authentication Protocol. It lets clients find authentication servers when they join a network. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2485 defines a DHCP option that gives a client URLs for User Authentication Protocol servers. Because DHCP has no authentication mechanism in the described system, a forged option could point a client to a rogue service.

subtitle: A DHCP option that provides URLs for User Authentication Protocol servers.

tldr.problem: A UAP client configured through DHCP needs an authentication-service address that can include a port and path, not only a server IP address.
tldr.mechanism: The DHCP option carries one or more URLs for UAP services, separated by ASCII spaces.
tldr.outcome: Clients can receive a list of authentication-service locations, but DHCP does not authenticate the source of that list and a forged option can redirect a client.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 2485's status as Proposed Standard. The RFC defines a DHCP option for locating User Authentication Protocol servers and describes a redirection risk.

sections.title: Locating a UAP Authentication Service
sections.content:
The User Authentication Protocol (UAP) lets a client authenticate using a basic mechanism or a secure form carried in an SSLv3 session. In either case, the client needs the service's IP address and port, and some implementations may also need a path.

Many UAP clients have little local configuration and receive settings through DHCP when they boot. Existing DHCP options could provide web-server addresses but not a full URL with port and path, so the RFC defines an option carrying URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: A client needs to know where its authentication service is located. This DHCP option can provide the full URL, including a port or path when needed.

sections.title: The URL List Option
sections.content:
The option contains one or more URLs for servers that process UAP authentication requests. URLs are separated by the ASCII space character, and the option uses code 98.

If a URL omits its port, the default is 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS. If it omits its path, the assumed path is /uap.
sections.plainLanguage: The option gives the client a list of service URLs. The RFC defines default ports and a default path when those parts are left out.

sections.title: A Forged DHCP Option Can Mislead a Client
sections.content:
The RFC notes that DHCP provides no authentication or security mechanism in the described setting. A forged or compromised option could direct a client to a rogue UAP service.

The document says that even secure UAP authentication does not protect against this kind of redirection. Its discussion points to environmental assumptions in the referenced Network Computing Client standard as the mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: A client cannot rely on this option to prove that a server is trustworthy. If an attacker changes the DHCP response, the client may contact a rogue authentication service.
